text:
“Open the door,” I told him, wondering who could be coming to my home at such an hour, and not daring to believe that it might be Marguerite.

“Sir,” Joseph said to me when he returned, “it is two ladies.”

“It is we, Armand,” a voice called out to me, which I recognized as Prudence’s.

I came out of my bedroom.

Prudence, standing, was looking at the few curiosities in my drawing room; Marguerite, seated on the sofa, was deep in thought.

When I entered, I went over to her, knelt down, took both her hands, and, deeply moved, said to her:

“Forgive me.”

She kissed me on the forehead and said:

“That makes three times already that I have forgiven you.”

“I was going to leave tomorrow.”

“How can my visit change your decision? I have not come to prevent you from leaving Paris. I have come because I did not have time during the day to answer you, and because I did not want to leave you thinking that I was angry with you. Besides, Prudence did not want me to come; she said that I might be disturbing you.”

“You disturb me—you, Marguerite! How could you?”

“Well! You might have had a woman here with you,” Prudence replied, “and it would not have been amusing for her to see two more arrive.”

During this observation of Prudence’s, Marguerite was watching me attentively.

“My dear Prudence,” I replied, “you do not know what you are saying.”

“The thing is, your apartment is very charming,” Prudence retorted; “may one see the bedroom?”

“Yes.”

Prudence went into my bedroom, less to inspect it than to make amends for the foolish thing she had just said and to leave Marguerite and me alone.

“Why did you bring Prudence?” I then asked her.

“Because she was with me at the theatre, and because, when I left here, I wanted to have someone to accompany me.”

“Was I not here?”

“Yes; but apart from the fact that I did not want to disturb you, I was quite sure that, on coming as far as my door, you would ask to come up to my rooms, and, as I could not grant you that, I did not want you to leave with the right to reproach me for a refusal.”

“And why could you not receive me?”

“Because I am watched very closely, and the slightest suspicion could do me the greatest harm.”

“Is that truly the only reason?”

“If there were another, I would tell you; we are past keeping secrets from one another.”

“Come now, Marguerite, I do not want to take several paths to arrive at what I want to say to you. Frankly, do you love me a little?”

“Very much.”

“Then why did you deceive me?”

“My friend, if I were the Duchess So-and-so, if I had an income of two hundred thousand livres, if I were your mistress and had another lover besides you, you would have the right to ask me why I deceive you; but I am Mademoiselle Marguerite Gautier, I have debts of forty thousand francs, not a penny to my name, and I spend a hundred thousand francs a year; your question becomes pointless and my answer unnecessary.”

“That is fair,” I said, letting my head fall upon Marguerite’s knees; “but I love you like a madman.”

“Well then, my friend, you should have loved me a little less or understood me a little better. Your letter caused me a great deal of pain. If I had been free, to begin with I would not have received the count the day before yesterday, or, having received him, I would have come to ask you for the forgiveness you were asking of me just now, and from then on I would have had no lover but you. For a moment I thought I might grant myself that happiness for six months; you would not have it; you insisted on knowing the means, and, good God, the means were easy enough to guess. In employing them, I was making a greater sacrifice than you think. I could have said to you: I need twenty thousand francs; you were in love with me, and you would have found them, at the risk of reproaching me for them later. I preferred to owe you nothing; you did not understand that delicacy, for it is one. Women like us, when we still have a little heart left, give words and things a scope and significance unknown to other women; I therefore repeat to you that, on Marguerite Gautier’s part, the means she found of paying her debts without asking you for the money needed to do so was an act of delicacy from which you ought to benefit without saying anything. If you had only met me today, you would be only too happy with what I was promising you, and you would not ask me what I did the day before yesterday. We are sometimes forced to purchase satisfaction for our souls at the expense of our bodies, and we suffer far more when, afterward, that satisfaction escapes us.”

I listened to Marguerite and gazed at her with admiration. When I thought that this marvelous creature, whose feet I would once have longed to kiss, was consenting to let me count for something in her thoughts, to give me a part in her life, and that I was still not content with what she gave me, I wondered whether man’s desire has any bounds when, having been satisfied as swiftly as mine had been, it still reaches for something else.

“It is true,” she continued; “we creatures of chance have capricious desires and inconceivable loves. We give ourselves now for one thing, now for another. There are men who would ruin themselves without obtaining anything from us, and there are others who have us for a bouquet. Our heart has its whims; they are its only diversion and its only excuse. I gave myself to thee more quickly than to any man, I swear it to thee; why? Because, seeing me spit blood, thou tookest my hand, because thou wept, because thou art the only human creature who was willing to pity me. I am going to tell thee something foolish, but I once had a little dog that looked at me very sadly when I coughed; it is the only being I have ever loved.

“When it died, I wept more than at my mother’s death. It is true that she had beaten me for twelve years of her life. Well, I loved thee at once as much as my dog. If men knew what they could obtain with a tear, they would be loved more, and we would be less ruinous to them.”
